subject: redPanda
pitch: A red panda balancing on a mossy branch. Rusty red fur on its back, a black belly and legs, a round white face with red tear marks running from the eyes, white-rimmed pointed ears, a little black nose, and a big fluffy tail with bold cream and ginger rings. It holds a bamboo shoot in one paw and looks delighted.
reasoning:
I'm planning out the module structure for building a red panda model on a mossy branch with bamboo, reviewing the SDK's builder API for joints, chains, and grouping to figure out the right construction approach.

There's also a rich set of primitives for shaping geometry—parts, sweeps, rods, spikes, lofts, surfaces, decals, and lathes—plus posing and material helpers, so I'm mapping out which of these fit best for the panda's fur, branch texture, and bamboo shoot details.

I'm noting the texture library (mottle, spots, stripes, patches, grain, noise, cells) and procedural path tools (rng, frame, limb with bends, splines) that I'll use for coat patterns and limb posing. The key structural insight is that the module exports a default build function returning the builder's root object, plus a meta object with name and description, so I'm setting up that export pattern and importing the necessary builder utilities before sketching out the red panda's actual proportions.

Thinking through real red panda sizing—body roughly 0.6m nose to rump, tail around 0.45m, shoulder height near 0.3m—and the placement constraint that everything must rest at y=0. Since the branch is scenery rather than a separate scene element, I'm treating it as a fallen branch or log lying along the ground so the panda can balance on it while the whole composition still touches the floor naturally.

I'm deciding to make the branch a horizontal limb whose radius determines its bottom height, keeping that bottom at y=0, with mossy green mottling and a few side twigs for detail without overcomplicating the model. For the pose, I'm picturing the red panda standing upright on top of the branch gripping it with its feet, body held semi-upright in that characteristic red panda stance, tail hanging down behind.

Scaling things out in meters, I'm thinking the top of the head should sit around 0.45m, with the branch itself around 0.09m radius lifting the panda's feet off the ground slightly, possibly supported by a tapered stump at one end for more character and stability, though I want to keep the geometry from getting too complex.

Orientation-wise, I'm deciding whether the branch should run along X or Z relative to the panda's forward-facing direction — placing it perpendicular to the panda's facing lets the animal straddle it naturally like a real red panda balancing sideways on a branch while still turning its face toward the viewer, which feels like the more iconic, readable pose.

I'm settling on a cute upright pose — body tilted back slightly, one paw holding bamboo and the other raised for balance, tail curving behind over the branch, head tilted up with happy crescent eyes and open smiling mouth. Now I'm moving into planning the actual geometry coordinates in meters, with Y as up and Z as forward.

I'm working out the branch and support structure: the branch runs along Z and needs to be elevated, so I'm considering adding a tapered stump at one end to lift it off the ground, giving the "balancing" feel rather than just resting on a fallen log.

Now I'm sketching the overall silhouette and color palette — rusty red back, black belly and legs, white face with red tear marks, cream ringed tail, plus mossy patches on the branch and a bamboo shoot for extra detail. I'm also working out body proportions for the red panda, setting shoulder height and body length so the legs straddle the branch naturally with paws resting on top.

For the pose, I'm positioning the panda crouched on the branch with front paws gripping it, one paw bringing bamboo toward its mouth while the other extends out for balance, and the ringed tail sweeping up and out behind for a dynamic counterbalance.

Now I'm turning to the skeleton rig itself. Since I can't test the SDK directly, I need to stick to well-understood joint and chain constructs to avoid runtime errors — defining a root joint near the pelvis, then building out spine, neck, head, jaw, tail, leg, and arm chains with careful positioning along a catmull spline from rump to shoulders to neck.

I'm reconsidering the spine as a chain with named joints along a catmull path, mapping names like "spine1", "spine2", "chest", with a tip joint for "neck", then attaching "head" to "neck" with its own position and aim direction. Given time constraints, I'm deciding the visual render matters more than rig perfection, so I should keep the joint structure functional but not over-engineer it.

Now I'm working out the actual numeric layout for the panda: positioning the branch using a tapered radius along a curved catmull path, figuring out where its bottom edge sits, and planning a supporting stump underneath at ground level so the branch doesn't float unsupported.

I'll build the branch path using a smooth catmull curve with tapered radius and faceted low-poly sides, with rounded ends to look like cut wood. For the surface, I want bark texture with grain blending into mossy green on the upward-facing surfaces, using noise and smoothstep to make the transition look natural rather than mechanical.

I'm scanning through the rest of the module exports to check for naming collisions — frame, distribute, math, path, surface, ik, sugar, sweep, texture, bake, rig, region, membrane, outline, parts, cards, decal, and skeleton all seem to export distinct, non-overlapping names, so no conflicts there.

For the bamboo shoot, I'm planning a tapered lathe profile for a pale green/cream cylinder with a pointed tip, maybe adding a couple small leaf-sheath slabs for detail, then positioning it held upright in the panda's right paw near chest/mouth height.

Switching to the body itself, I'm thinking of a sweep along a spine path with a width/height radius function to get a slender, fluffy red panda torso — narrower at hips, deeper through the chest — using modest polygon counts (8-12 sides) since this is a stylized low-poly build. I'll define the spine path running from the rump back around z=-0.22 up to the shoulders near z=0.

For skinning the body across the spine chain, I realize `loft` with stations (rump, hip, waist, chest, shoulder, neck base) is the better tool than a plain sweep, since it lets me set width/height per station and bind the mesh to the spine joints via the `bone` option so the body deforms naturally with the skeleton.

Now I'm thinking through the fur coloring: countershaded red-rust back with black belly and legs, like a real red panda, plus facial features — white face with cream muzzle, red tear-mark streaks running from the inner eyes down to the mouth, a dark nose, and red-rimmed pointed ears with a white inner rim. I'm sketching the head as a slightly flattened rounded shape to carry these markings.

For the head geometry itself, I'm weighing a simple scaled sphere against a swept/lathed form, settling on a basic sphere part with a non-uniform scale since it already provides usable UV coordinates for painting the face. I'm defining a face mask using the point and normal data to figure out where the white muzzle, tear marks, and other markings should land relative to the head's center.

I'm also sanity-checking the texel density math: with a shared paint sheet at 2048px and roughly half a square meter of total surface area across the body parts, I'm estimating around 2400-4000 texels per meter, meaning each paint call needs to stay cheap since it could run millions of times across the sheet.

Given the number of paint calls could run into the tens of seconds in a browser, I'm weighing dropping to a 1024px sheet, which still gives sub-millimeter precision and plenty of detail for fur and face marks, while cutting the total work roughly in proportion to the smaller sheet size.

I should also account for bounding-box inflation on curved charts plus the padding texels on each side. For paint functions I want to keep per-call cost low, avoiding heavy allocations and reading x/y directly when possible, while supporting flexible color return types. For tail coloring, I can use the sweep parameter to create alternating cream and ginger bands along the tail's length using a bands-style option.

Using bands rather than paint gives flat-colored, crisp ring segments with clean splits at each edge, which fits the bold cream-and-ginger ring look better than a smooth gradient paint. I'm working out the actual band sequence along the tail — starting from the base with alternating ginger and cream segments at roughly even intervals toward the tip.

For colors, I want cream distinct from the rusty-red body tone, so I'm using a warm cream and a clearly separate ginger-orange, making sure the body's rust color doesn't blend visually with the tail rings. Then I'm shaping the tail path itself as a long, bushy curve rising from the rump and arcing upward and back, giving it that classic held-out red panda tail silhouette with a slight curling tip.

I'm working out the tail's radius profile so it bulges in the middle and tapers at the tip for a fluffy look, then moving on to leg placement and darkening the limbs to the typical black-brown red panda coloring.

Now I'm structuring the leg chains as polylines running from shoulder to elbow to wrist for the arms, and hip to knee to ankle to foot for the hind legs, naming each joint segment so the pose reads correctly with feet planted on top of the branch.

For simplicity I'm leaning toward building limbs as joints connected by rigid capsules, since a Joint naturally carries bone weights for attachment. But for smoother skinning across chains and sweeps, I'm considering using a sweep along a chain of joints with a given radius instead, which would better suit limbs, necks, and tails.

For legs specifically, I'd create a chain with a sequence of path points parented to the hips joint, then sweep a radius profile along that chain so it bends smoothly through the joints. The rig can stay in a static bind pose since this is a stylized panda model and doesn't need posing.

Now I'm thinking through the root joint placement—putting "hips" near the pelvis and building a spine chain from there up to the neck. The tricky part is the chain's first joint coincides with the hips position, so I'm considering whether to just let the spine chain start directly from hips rather than duplicating a separate root joint.

I realize creating a separate root joint and then a spine chain starting at the same position would create a duplicate zero-length bone. That's technically harmless since the rig just needs one root joint, so root→hips as a zero-length bone is an acceptable solution to the chicken-and-egg problem.

I'm sketching a joint chain for the spine — hips, waist, chest, neck, head, each parented to the previous — and weighing whether to build the body as a sweep over individual joints versus a named chain with a role. Either approach works, but using chains with explicit names feels redundant with a separate root joint, so I'm leaning toward just defining the spine as a joint hierarchy directly rather than wrapping it in a chain abstraction.

I'm settling on building the body path as a catmull spline through the joint positions, then using closestT to map each joint onto the spline for the sweep's bone spans, which should give smooth blending across the spine without duplicating joint definitions.

For the head, instead of folding it into the body sweep, I'll just attach a rigid part geometry directly to a "head" joint and let its rotation follow that joint's aim direction, which simplifies things considerably.

For the legs, I'm thinking of each limb as its own chain built from a polyline through hip, knee, ankle, and toe points, parented to the hip bone so the first leg joint sits at the hip socket and inherits correctly from the body.

Now I'm sweeping each leg chain into a tube using its span joints and weights, then adding a small flattened black sphere at the tip of each chain as a foot pad resting on the branch -- front paws dark with maybe cream toes to match a red panda's look, and I'm sketching out the overall standing pose with hind feet gripping the branch and one front paw raised holding bamboo while the other extends for balance before working out the actual branch centerline coordinates.

I'm figuring out the rock's placement so its top surface meets the underside of the branch where it dips near z=-0.12, then calculating foot height on the branch top and setting the hip, chest, and leg lengths so the proportions read correctly -- hips around y=0.47, feet at y=0.32, chest at y=0.52 -- before starting to lay out the spine joint coordinates for the body.

Working out body segment radii at each spine joint (rump, hips, waist, chest, neck) so the torso tapers naturally, then figuring out how to map these radii onto the sweep's parameter since the catmull path knots don't align evenly with joint indices -- considering switching to a stations-based loft approach instead for more direct control.

Since bone weights come from the joint list directly, passing explicit bone data makes path weights irrelevant, so I'll use plain number arrays for station positions to keep things simple. For bone spans, each joint's closest-t on the path determines its span, so I need the body stations and bone list (hips, waist, chest, neck) to line up properly, with the neck station ending where it tucks into the head.

I'm defining full width/height values per station since the sweep halves them internally -- rump, hips, waist, chest, and neck each get their own position and size, with hips being the widest point for haunches and chest the deepest for the fluffy front. The rump sits behind the hips joint but isn't itself a joint, so it just inherits the hips' bone weights since it's before the first joint boundary in the span logic.

Now I'm working out the fur coloring: the belly and legs should be black/dark, the back rusty-red, blended smoothly based on the normal's y-component so the transition between back and belly isn't a hard edge.

Since paints can't be mixed directly, I need to sample each nested paint's color at a point and blend the resulting RGB values using the belly weight as the interpolation factor.

Now I'm working out the head geometry: placing the head center and radius, then defining a local coordinate frame relative to it so I can mask facial features. I'm sketching the white muzzle/cheek region as a soft-edged ellipse facing forward, with the forehead and crown colored rust-red, ears as separate shapes, and eyes marked as closed slits.

For the eyes, I'm deciding on happy closed crescents—small upward-arching dark strokes positioned symmetrically on the face—working out the math for an arc shape bulging upward (∩-like) so the dark stroke appears only within a thin band around that curve near the eye center.

I'm weighing whether to build the eyes as painted texture versus actual swept-arc geometry on the head surface, and leaning toward the paint approach since it's more robust to the sphere's surface mapping. I'm also considering adding an open mouth with a tongue to really sell the "delighted" expression.

Since the contract requires creatures to have separate upper and lower jaw pieces so the mouth can open, I'm planning a jaw joint hinged behind the mouth, parented to the head, with a cream or white lower jaw ellipsoid and a dark painted interior to suggest the open mouth cavity.

Working out the rotation math so a positive rotation about the X-axis correctly swings the jaw tip downward and forward when posed open.

I'm weighing two approaches: using a pose rotation on the jaw joint versus just baking the open angle directly into the jaw's rest geometry and orientation, leaning toward defining the jaw joint's aim direction so it naturally points down-forward from the hinge toward the chin.

For the actual geometry I'm considering a flattened ellipsoid part positioned at the chin point as the lower jaw rather than a rod or sweep, since that reads better stylistically than a stick-like shape. The upper jaw stays rigid as part of the head, and I'm noting the lower jaw should be painted white to match the muzzle coloring typical of a red panda, with a darker tone for the mouth interior.

For the mouth cavity, I'll just paint a dark ellipse directly onto the head sphere's front-lower surface to simulate the open mouth gap, rather than adding separate interior geometry, and then add a small pink tongue accent within that dark region for detail.

For the nose, I'm placing a small black ellipsoid part at the muzzle tip on the head, scaled slightly flatter to look like a proper button nose rather than a protruding snout — the round white face comes from a paint mask on the head sphere itself (white front disc, red elsewhere) instead of a separate muzzle geometry, keeping the short red panda snout look with the nose and tear marks painted directly onto that white region.

Now I'm figuring out the tear marks: thin red streaks running from just below each eye down toward the mouth corners, computed as a tapered stroke along a line segment with distance-based falloff. For the ears, I'm thinking through a pointed, upright shape with a white rim — likely using an extruded outline for the rounded-triangle ear silhouette, then painting a rust-red fill with a white edge band, though getting the rim to read correctly through the paint function surface coordinates will take some care.

Working out the ear placement and orientation on the head, positioning each ear's local plane so it faces sideways-up with the right tilt, then defining the triangle points for the ear geometry relative to that base frame.

Adjusting the ear base position slightly inward and setting its orientation vectors for height and outward tilt. Now I'm working out where to place the bamboo shoot in the panda's paw—deciding whether to hold it raised near the face or lower against the chest to avoid it clipping through the head geometry, leaning toward a more natural "eating" pose with the paw near the chest.

I'm checking the geometry to confirm the bamboo shoot's path clears the head sphere by computing distances from the shoot's base, midpoint, and tip to the head center, confirming they all stay outside the head radius. Now I'm setting up how to generate the bamboo shoot as a lathe shape, defining its tapered cross-section radii at the base, bulge point, and tip, with the lathe axis aligned to the shoot's tilted direction.

For coloring, I'm planning to apply a stripe paint pattern along the shoot's axis using green and cream tones, and layering in a brownish-purple leaf sheath near the base using a height-based condition in the paint function.

Beyond coloring, I'm thinking about adding texture through moss clumps and small leaves as card elements, though SVG-based leaf textures won't render properly outside a browser environment since they rely on DOM parsing.

If `document` is undefined, the texture would just be blank and transparent, making cards invisible but not breaking anything, so I'll proceed with using a leaf card for bamboo leaves and possibly moss tufts. For tinting, I want to pass "#ffffff" so the texture renders as drawn, and I'm figuring out how to use `b.cards` with frames from `b.surface(branch).scatter()` to scatter moss tufts onto branch surfaces.

I'm thinking of placing moss as small upright cards where the surface normal faces mostly upward, filtering hits by their y-component. I'm plotting the curve points so the tail arcs backward and slightly down before curling upward and forward for a balanced pose, checking proximity to the branch position to avoid overlap.
